regions.evidence: Satellite (spring 2021, outside the 2020-11 window): r1 is a ~2.5-2.8 m band whose left edge lines up with the end of the opposing WB stop bar. That stop bar stops at the left edge of r1, and the WB lanes with down-pointing arrows lie further left. r1 has no lane paint and no vehicles; the only line nearby is a faint dark line inside r2 for the first ~7 m. The whole scene is in deep building shadow, so a median kerb or tree trunks cannot be resolved directly, and the band's brightness is barely different from the pavement. Street views (2020-11, inside the window): at 22.7 m and 51.5 m the away views show a raised planted median with a kerb, grass, leaf litter and a row of trees between the WB carriageway and the EB travel lane, with a yellow edge line on the EB side. The 101.9 m toward view shows the same median on the right. Exactly one EB travel lane runs beside it. r1 is the only strip of median width between the WB stop bar end and the EB lane. If it were pavement, r1+r2 would form a ~7 m single lane, which the street views do not show. So r1 is read as the median. The exact kerb position is inferred, not seen.

visual_refs.finding: WB stop bar ending at r1's left edge
unmarked shadowed band with no vehicles
planted median with kerb, trees and yellow edge line left of the EB lane
same planted median with trees further downstream

regions.evidence: Satellite: uniform asphalt about 4 m wide between the median band (r1) and a continuous solid white line on its right. The line runs from the crosswalk to the far end of the section. The crosswalk at the junction end runs across r2. No arrows are readable, and no vehicles are present. Everything is in shadow. Street views (2020-11): at 22.7 m and 51.5 m the camera stands in a single EB travel lane between the median's yellow edge line and a solid white line. The 22.7 m and 51.5 m toward views and the 101.9 m toward view show the same single lane alongside the median. No pavement arrow appears in this lane near the camera. Correspondence is by physical sequence (median, travel lane, white-line pair, parking, kerb), not ordinal. The satellite date (2021) is later than the window; the GSV dates fall in it, and the two agree.

visual_refs.finding: solid white line forming r2's right edge, continuous from the crosswalk
crosswalk spanning r2 at the junction end
single EB travel lane between yellow edge line and solid white line
single travel lane beside the median continuing downstream

regions.evidence: Satellite: a ~1.5-1.7 m strip between two parallel solid white lines that run continuously from the crosswalk past the parked cars. It lies between the travel lane r2 and the parking row. No symbol is legible in the shadowed satellite. Street views (2020-11): every away/toward pair shows a strip between two white lines separating the travel lane from the parking lane. At 22.7 m a worn white marking lies inside it, part of a bicycle symbol or arrow. At 101.9 m (toward view) the strip carries a clear bicycle glyph and a straight arrow pointing in the EB travel direction. It is a bicycle lane; the arrow is a bicycle direction marking, not a motor-vehicle turn arrow. The 101.9 m view is downstream of the satellite polygon, but line continuity links the two.

visual_refs.finding: pair of parallel solid white lines bounding the strip
worn bicycle marking between the two white lines
bicycle symbol in the strip
straight arrow pointing in EB travel direction (toward camera)

regions.evidence: Satellite: right of the white-line pair, a row of parked cars sits end to end at the upstream end of the section, within the left ~2.5 m of r4. This is a kerbside parking lane. The crosswalk ends about 2.5 m right of the line pair, marking the kerb. The rest of r4 (~3.5 m) lies beyond the kerb: a darker band and then the edge of a building roof, so r4 extends past the true kerb onto the grass strip and sidewalk. No cars are visible in r4 between the junction and the parked row. That part may be a no-parking zone near the crossing, but it shows no travel-lane paint. Street views (2020-11): at 22.7 m and 51.5 m, parked cars and a van stand at the right kerb beyond the bike lane, with a grass strip, benches and sidewalk behind them. At 101.9 m the toward view shows the same parking strip between the bike lane and the kerb. Not a travel lane.

visual_refs.finding: row of parked cars right of the white-line pair
band beyond the kerb (grass strip/sidewalk) inside r4's right part
parked van and cars at the right kerb beyond the bike lane
parked car at the kerb right of the bike lane

notes: Satellite (spring 2021) lies outside the 2020-11 target window and is entirely in building shadow. Kerbs and the median edge are inferred from the stop-bar end, crosswalk extent and line positions rather than seen as crisp edges.

All six street views are 2020-11, inside the window. Each away/toward pair comes from one panorama, so there are three original sources (22.7, 51.5, 101.9 m). They show a consistent layout: planted median, one EB travel lane, a two-line bicycle lane, a kerbside parking lane, kerb.
The camera metadata ('nominal outgoing side') was checked against the imagery. The cameras are in the EB carriageway itself: median on the left looking away, kerb with parking on the right.
The 101.9 m away view shows dashed lines and a median end approaching the next intersection, beyond the regions. It does not bear on the region classes here.

regions.evidence: Satellite (spring 2021, after the target window; geometry only): r1's left edge follows the bright centre line, with the opposing approach's turn arrows beyond it. Its left ~3.5 m is unmarked asphalt with nothing in it. Its right ~2 m holds three cars parked end to end along the kerb, beyond which are sidewalk/plaza and buildings. Street views, all 2020-11 and inside the target window: (1) 29.7 m, away and toward headings of one panorama. The camera is on the SB side (double yellow line on its left when facing away from the junction). It shows one SB travel lane, then a solid white edge line, then cars parked at the right kerb (a Mini and a van), then the sidewalk. (2) 59.5 m, one panorama. Facing away, the single SB lane runs straight to the granite kerb and brick sidewalk, with no parking line. Facing toward the junction, a white parking edge line begins just ahead of the camera, with a car parked beyond it near the junction. So the parking strip in r1 starts between about 60 m and the junction. (3) 113.4 m: despite the metadata, this camera is on the opposing NB carriageway. The double yellow line is on its right facing away, oncoming cars are in its lane, and NB bike-lane/buffer markings are on its right facing toward. Across the centre line it shows a single SB lane with an oncoming sedan, so it supports one SB lane but not r1's exact extent. Conclusion: r1 is real roadway carrying one SB motor lane. However, its right ~2 m (about 36% of its 5.5 m width) is a kerbside parking lane, not travel pavement; a split there would give one motor lane plus shoulder_or_parking. No arrows are visible on the receiving lane.

row of parked cars in the right ~2 m of r1 along the kerb
double yellow centre line on the camera's left (camera on SB side)
single SB travel lane between the centre line and the white edge line

parking edge line beginning just ahead of the 59.5 m camera
car parked at the kerb beyond the edge line, toward the junction
single SB lane running directly to the granite kerb downstream, no parking line
across the double yellow line from the opposing-side camera: one SB lane with an oncoming car

notes: Temporal basis: all six street views are 2020-11, inside the target window, and give the direct confirmation: one SB travel lane, with kerbside parking near the junction. The spring-2021 satellite is later context; it shows the same arrangement (cars parked in r1's right part), so no change between the dates is evident.

The two headings at each street-view location come from one panorama, so there are three original street-view sources at 29.7 m, 59.5 m and 113.4 m. The 113.4 m panorama is on the opposing carriageway, contrary to its 'nominal outgoing side' metadata, and supports the target only across the centre line.
r1's width (5.5 m) covers the travel lane plus the parking strip; only the left ~3.5 m is motor travel pavement.

regions.evidence: Satellite (spring 2021, after the 2020-11 window): continuous grey asphalt from just beyond the crosswalk. On the left is the kerb of a raised median island with a bench/shelter structure and planters at its rounded nose; r1's left edge follows that kerb and the nose curve. On the right is the left line of a hatched painted buffer. Cross-section profiles on the sunlit part show no lane line inside r1 between the island kerb and the buffer line: one wide general-traffic lane, roughly 4.5-5 m (scale estimated from vehicle length). The upper ~35% lies in building shadow; the island kerb line and the pavement continue there. Street views (2020-11, in the window): at 34.6 m the away view shows the camera in a single wide WB lane between a yellow edge line along the raised grass median with trees and a hatched buffer with white flexible posts. The 34.6 m toward view shows the same single lane back to the crosswalk. At 54.1 m the lane continues as one lane where the median jogs (S-bend). Matched by physical sequence (median kerb, lane, hatched buffer, bike lane, kerb), not by ordinal. The 104 m views show a wider multi-lane cross-section with dashed lines, beyond this polygon; they do not change r1's single-lane reading near the junction.

visual_refs.finding: unmarked asphalt with no internal lane line
kerb of the raised median island forming r1's left edge
single WB travel lane between yellow edge line and hatched buffer
raised grass median with trees and yellow edge line on the left

regions.evidence: Satellite: a narrow strip (about 1 m) between two parallel solid white lines, with diagonal hatch bars painted between them at regular intervals along its whole length. This is a painted buffer, not a travel facility. Street views (2020-11): at 34.6 m (away and toward) the same two-line buffer with diagonal hatching carries white flexible delineator posts and separates the travel lane from the kerbside bicycle lane.

visual_refs.finding: two solid white lines with diagonal hatch bars
hatched buffer with white flexible delineator posts

regions.evidence: Satellite: a paved strip (about 1.7-1.9 m) between the buffer's right line and the kerb. Beyond the kerb are a light sidewalk with a row of round reddish planters, granite-edged tree pits and further sidewalk. Inside the strip near the junction is a bicycle-lane glyph with a straight arrow ahead of it pointing in the WB travel direction. The arrow is a bike-lane direction marking, not a motor turn arrow. Street views (2020-11): at 34.6 m the strip beyond the post-lined buffer runs along the kerb, with parked bikes and a sidewalk beyond. At 54.1 m the kerbside lane continues with green paint and bicycle markings. The width, buffer and markings fit a buffered bicycle lane; it is too narrow for a car lane.

visual_refs.finding: bicycle glyph and straight direction arrow inside the strip
kerb, then sidewalk with round planters immediately right of the strip
kerbside bicycle lane beyond the post-lined buffer

notes: All six street views are 2020-11, inside the target window, from three panoramas (34.6, 54.1, 104.0 m); the away/toward pairs are not independent. The satellite is spring 2021, later context; it agrees with the street views on all three regions.
The cameras are on the WB carriageway itself (median on the left looking away, kerb and bike lane on the right), so no across-median correspondence was needed.

An orange temporary lane-shift warning sign stands on the right sidewalk in the 34.6 m away view. Lane positions may have been temporarily altered at that time, though the paint seen matches the satellite.
Downstream (104 m) the carriageway widens to several lanes with dashed lines; that lies beyond these candidate regions.
